check:0:1.q: Why not “Let the agent that wrote the answer check it on…”?
check:0:1.a:
Asking the writer to check its own answer once more does get one thing right: a second look can catch a small slip, like a typo or a missing step.

But it misses the real problem in this question. The agent that wrote the answer still remembers the whole chat that produced it. It knows what it *meant* to say, so it reads that meaning into the answer. It shares the same blind spots that caused the mistake in the first place. That is why agents grading their own work tend to say "looks fine."

There is a second issue. The question says the checker already passes almost everything. That points to vague standards, not just to who is checking. Without concrete rules, any checker runs a quick look or two and declares victory. A self-check has no rules either, so it would be just as lenient, or worse.

The better option is "Give the checker a written checklist of pass or fail rules." It wins because clear rules like "cites a help article" or "no made-up order numbers" can actually fail, so the checker has to test for them instead of just nodding along.

judge.notes: Minor: the closing explanation runs to two sentences rather than one, and the claim that a self-check 'has no rules either, so it would be just as lenient, or worse' goes beyond what the lesson states.

check:0:2.q: Why not “Raise the round cap from 3 to 10”?
check:0:2.a:
Raising the cap sounds like "check harder," but it doesn't change how the checker judges anything.

Look at the problem again. The checker passes almost every answer. That means it reports 0 issues on the very first round. When that happens, the loop stops right away and calls the work clean. Rounds 2 through 10 never run. A bigger cap only matters when the checker keeps finding problems, and here it finds none.

So the cap isn't the weak spot. The weak spot is that the checker has no concrete rules. Without them, it skims, runs a test or two, and declares victory. That is the same "looks fine to me" habit you hoped a fresh checker would avoid.

What the option gets right: a round cap is worth tuning. Too low, and fixable work gets sent to a person too early. But that's a different problem from a checker that never fails anything.

"Give the checker a written checklist of pass or fail rules" is the right answer because it fixes the cause: clear rules that can really fail make the checker catch the wrong answers in the first place.

check:1:1.q: Why not “Keep going until the checker passes”?
check:1:1.a:
"Keep going until the checker passes" gets one thing right. The goal really is work with zero issues, and checking again after each fix is the core of the loop.

What it misses is that nothing promises the checker will ever pass. Some issues may be ones the fixer can't solve. For example, there may be no help article that fits the question, so "cites a help article" can fail every round. Without a cap, the loop could keep going forever. Each round calls a model again, so it also keeps costing time and money.

That is why the lesson says to cap the rounds and decide in advance what happens at the cap. In the example, the cap is 3. Once round 3 still finds issues, the loop has used up its allowed tries. The next step should already be chosen, not made up on the spot.

So the right answer is **"Do what you planned: warn, or ask a person."** It is better because it guarantees the loop ends, and the unfixed issues still get flagged instead of being hidden or chased endlessly.

check:1:2.q: Why not “Quietly return the last try as done”?
check:1:2.a:
"Quietly return the last try as done" gets one thing right. It respects the cap. The loop stops after round 3 instead of running forever, and the user still gets an answer.

What it misses is honesty. The checker just found 2 real problems. Calling the work "done" hides that. Whoever receives it, a customer or the next step in your system, will trust it as clean. In the help-center example, one of those issues could be a made-up order number. That goes straight to a customer with nothing to warn anyone.

It also throws away the checker's work. You built a fresh reviewer and a checklist with rules that can really fail. When they do fail, ignoring the result means the checker made no difference at the moment it mattered most.

The cap is not a sign that things are fine. It is a sign that you ran out of tries. So the outcome should say so.

"Do what you planned: warn, or ask a person" is better because the known issues travel with the result, so someone can see them and decide what to do.

check:2:0.q: Why not “Ask the agent if it is sure”?
check:2:0.a:
Asking the agent "are you sure?" does get one thing right. It adds a second look, and sometimes a second look catches a slip.

But it misses the main point of the lesson. It is the **same agent**, with the same chat history and the same blind spots. An agent asked to judge its own work tends to say the work is fine. So "are you sure?" usually just gets "yes."

It also keeps the check stuck in words. The checker in the question was fooled by an *explanation*. Asking for more confidence only produces more explanation. A clear, confident paragraph about a query is not proof that the query works. (A **query** is the request sent to a database to fetch data.)

That is why the right answer is "Run the query and look at the result." The checker gets real **evidence**, meaning something it can observe directly, instead of a claim.

Running the query is better because the result comes from the database, not from the agent, so it can actually fail when the query is wrong.

check:2:2.q: Why not “Ask for a longer explanation”?
check:2:2.a:
Asking for a longer explanation feels like a stricter check. It does get one thing right: more detail can sometimes expose a gap in the agent's reasoning that a short answer hid.

But it misses the main point of the lesson. A longer explanation is still the agent talking about its own work. The checker is still grading words, not results. An agent that wrote a wrong query can just as easily write a long, confident, wrong explanation of it. More words often make a mistake *harder* to spot, because the explanation sounds thorough.

This is the same trap as letting an agent grade itself. The checker should be fresh and should look at **evidence**. Evidence means something real you can inspect, like the actual output of the query, not a claim about what the output would be.

Running the query is better because the result either matches what the question asked for or it doesn't, so the check can genuinely fail no matter how convincing the explanation sounds.

explain:gotcha.q: Why does “Don't let it grade its own homework” matter?
explain:gotcha.a:
When an agent checks its own answer, it can still see its own reasoning. That reasoning is its **context**, meaning everything the model can see right now. Reading its own logic again, it finds the logic convincing. So it usually says "looks good." That's not lying. It's like proofreading your own essay: you read what you meant, not what you wrote.

A separate checker starts fresh. It sees only the finished work and a written checklist of pass or fail rules. It has no story about why the answer "must" be right. It just tests the work.

**What goes wrong when you skip this:** Say a help-center agent writes a reply that mentions "order #48213." Asked "Is this correct?", the same agent remembers deciding that number fit. It says yes. But the number was made up. A customer gets a fake order number and opens a confused support ticket.

A fresh checker with the rule "no made-up order numbers" would look the number up for real, perhaps with a tool like `run_query`. It wouldn't find it, so the check fails. That gets the reply fixed before anyone sees it.

learn:spot.q: How would I spot it going wrong?
learn:spot.a:
**Signs the checker isn't doing its job**

- **Everything passes on round 1.** If almost every answer comes back with 0 issues, the checker is probably rubber-stamping. It may be seeing the chat that made the work, or the checklist may be too vague to ever fail.
- **Quality drops in real use.** Your logs say "clean," but users still find made-up order numbers or missing help-article links.
- **Issue counts don't shrink.** In your traces (the step-by-step record of each run), the numbers bounce, like 3, then 3, then 4. That means the fixes aren't landing, or the checker is changing its mind.
- **Runs that never end, or cost spikes.** This points to no round cap, or a cap that isn't being checked.
- **Nothing happens at the cap.** A run hits round 3 with issues left, but no warning appears and no person sees it. The work just ships.
- **The checker never calls its tools.** It reads the agent's explanation instead of gathering real evidence, like running the query.

**Quickest check**

Hand the checker an answer you broke on purpose, such as one with a fake order number. It should fail it. If it passes, your checker is the problem.

judge.notes: No real problems; it is right at the ~200-word limit, so trimming a bullet would be safer.

learn:stops.a:
This method works well, but it needs extra care in a few situations.

**The checker is the same model as the worker.** The same model tends to make the same mistakes, so the checker may miss exactly what the worker missed. Use a different model for the checker, or lean on checks that use real evidence, like running the query.

**The rules can't really fail.** A rule like "the answer is helpful" is a judgment call, so the checker passes almost anything. Rewrite each rule as a clear yes-or-no test, like "cites a help article," and try the checklist on answers you know are bad.

**Fixes undo each other.** Fixing one issue can bring back an old one, so the issue count bounces around instead of shrinking. Keep the best attempt so far, and treat a round with no progress as a reason to stop and hand it to a person.

learn:term.a:
In this lesson, they are **the same thing**. "Checker," "verifier," and "critic" are three names for one role. The lesson says so: a checker is "often called a verifier or critic." Different teams and papers just pick different words.

**What that one role is.** A second agent that starts fresh. It sees only the finished work and a written checklist of pass-or-fail rules. It does not see the chat that produced the work. That fresh start matters, because an agent grading its own work tends to say it's fine.

**Everyday comparison.** Think of a restaurant. The cook makes the dish. A second person at the pass checks it against a card before it goes out. Whether you call that person the checker or the inspector, the job is the same.

**The lesson's example.** A help-center answer is checked against three rules:

- answers the question
- cites a help article
- no made-up order numbers

It goes through check, fix, check again, for at most 3 rounds. After round 3, one issue is still left, so it goes to a person with that issue noted.

judge.notes: No real problems. The restaurant term 'at the pass' may be unfamiliar to some beginners, and 'teams and papers' goes slightly beyond the lesson, but neither is wrong.

check:0:0.q: Why not “Pick the team: it passes 2 more tasks than one …”?
check:0:0.a:
"Pick the team" gets one thing right. The team really does pass more tasks: 8 instead of 6. If accuracy were free, that would settle it.

But accuracy isn't free here. The answer looks only at the pass count and ignores what those extra passes cost.

Work it out. The team costs $7 and one agent costs $1, so the team spends $6 more. It passes 2 more tasks. $6 divided by 2 is $3 for each extra pass. That's the **marginal cost**: the price of one more passed task.

Now compare that with what a pass is worth to you: $2. Picking the team means paying $3 to get something worth $2. You'd lose $1 on every extra pass.

Counting passes alone can't show this. Neither can cost per success alone. You need the extra dollars divided by the extra passes, set next to the value of a pass.

"Keep one agent: each extra pass costs $3, too much" is better because it weighs what each extra pass costs ($3) against what it's worth to you ($2), and the cost is higher.

check:0:2.q: Why not “Pick the team: its cost per success is still un…”?
check:0:2.a:
The fact in that option is true. The team spends $7 and passes 8 tasks, so its cost per success is $7 ÷ 8, about $0.88. That is under $1.

But it answers the wrong question. Cost per success tells you what one passed task costs on average. It does not tell you whether the team's *extra* passes are worth paying for. And "under $1" is not even a fair comparison: one agent's cost per success is $1 ÷ 6, about $0.17. So the team is already pricier on that measure too.

The number that decides it is the cost of each extra pass, also called the marginal cost:

- Extra dollars: $7 minus $1 is $6 more.
- Extra passes: 8 minus 6 is 2 more.
- $6 divided by 2 is $3 for each extra pass.

Each extra pass is worth $2 to you, but it costs $3. You would lose $1 on every extra task the team passes.

"Keep one agent: each extra pass costs $3, too much" is better because it compares what each extra pass costs with what it is worth to you, and that is the comparison that settles the choice.

check:1:0.q: Why not “8, all of the team's passes”?
check:1:0.a:
Dividing by 8 gets one thing right: the top of the fraction is still the extra dollars, the $5.40 the team costs beyond one agent.

The problem is the bottom. Dividing by 8 spreads that $5.40 over all 8 of the team's passes. But 6 of those 8 are passes one agent would have given you anyway, for just $0.50. The extra money didn't buy them.

So $5.40 divided by 8 comes out to about $0.68. That makes each extra pass look about four times cheaper than it really is. A low number like that could talk you into the team when one agent was the better deal.

It also sits close to cost per success, which is the whole bill divided by all passes. For the team that's $5.90 divided by 8, about $0.74. That number answers a different question: what one passed task costs on average. It doesn't tell you what the *extra* passes cost.

Dividing by 2, just the extra passes, is better because it matches the extra dollars to the only passes those dollars actually bought: $5.40 for 2 passes, so $2.70 each.

check:1:2.a:
Dividing by 6 is a natural slip. The number 6 does matter here. You use it once, to subtract from the team's 8. But it's the wrong thing to divide by.

Think about what the extra $5.40 actually buys. One agent already passes 6 tasks for $0.50. You don't need the team for those 6. The extra money only gets you the tasks one agent couldn't pass, and there are 2 of them.

If you divide $5.40 by 6, you get $0.90. That spreads the extra cost over passes you already had for cheap. So each extra pass looks much cheaper than it really is. You might then pick the team when one agent was the better deal.

Dividing by 2 gives $2.70 for each extra pass. That is the real price of what the team adds.

"2, just the extra passes" is better because it divides the extra dollars by exactly what those dollars bought, and nothing else.

judge.notes: No major problems. The line saying the extra money buys 'the tasks one agent couldn't pass' is slightly loose, because the lesson defines extra passes as a difference in counts, but it doesn't contradict the lesson.

check:2:0.q: Why not “How many helpers the team uses”?
check:2:0.a:
"How many helpers the team uses" gets one thing right. More helpers usually means more model calls, and more calls usually means a bigger bill. So it hints that the team costs more.

But it is only a hint. It is a head count, not a price. Two helpers that write long answers can cost more than five helpers that write short ones. What you pay depends on tokens (the small chunks of text a model reads and writes), and the number of helpers doesn't tell you that.

It also doesn't connect to the 3 extra passes. Say you know the team uses 4 helpers. You still can't tell whether those 3 passes cost $3 or $300. So you can't decide if the team is worth it.

The question you actually need answered is "what am I paying for each extra pass?" A helper count can't answer it.

"What each extra pass costs in dollars" is better because it puts a real price on exactly those 3 extra passes, so you can compare it with what one more passed task is worth to you.

judge.notes: No real problems. The claim that more helpers usually means more calls and a bigger bill goes beyond the lesson but does not contradict it, and the answer stays at roughly 185 words.

check:2:1.q: Why not “How long each helper's prompt is”?
check:2:1.a:
Prompt length isn't a bad thing to notice. Each helper's prompt is turned into tokens (small chunks of text the model reads and bills you for). Longer prompts mean more input tokens on every call, so prompt length does push the bill up.

But it's only one ingredient of the cost, not the cost itself. It leaves out the model's output tokens. It leaves out how many calls each helper makes, and the runs that failed but still cost money. It isn't in dollars either. So you can't hold it up against "3 more passes" and decide anything.

The question you need answered is: "Are those 3 extra passes worth what they cost?" Prompt length can't tell you that. A team with short prompts can still be expensive if its helpers call the model many times.

The right answer is "What each extra pass costs in dollars." It takes the team's extra spending and divides it by the 3 extra passes. That gives you one price you can compare directly with what a passed task is worth to you.

explain:gotcha.q: Why does “Divide by successes, not by runs” matter?
explain:gotcha.a:
Every run costs money, even the ones that fail. The model still reads the prompt and writes an answer, and you pay for those tokens. (Tokens are the small chunks of text a model is billed by.) A failed run gives you nothing to show for that spend.

If you divide the bill by runs, failures look free. A design that fails a lot can then look like the bargain.

Here's a small example. Same 10 tasks:

- Design A costs $0.10 per run and passes 2 of 10.
- Design B costs $0.30 per run and passes 9 of 10.

By runs, A looks three times cheaper. Now divide by successes:

- A: $1.00 total ÷ 2 passes = $0.50 per finished task.
- B: $3.00 total ÷ 9 passes ≈ $0.33 per finished task.

The "cheap" design actually costs more for each job it gets done.

In real work, this mistake leads you to pick the wrong design. Your budget forecast comes out too low. Failed tasks also need a human to fix them or a rerun, and you pay for those too.

judge.notes: The arithmetic checks out and nothing breaks the rules. The closing line about humans fixing failed tasks goes beyond the lesson, but it doesn't contradict it.

learn:spot.q: How would I spot it going wrong?
learn:spot.a:
**Warning signs the idea was skipped**

- The team was picked because its pass rate went up, and nobody wrote down what each extra pass cost.
- Cost per success looks fine, maybe under a dollar, yet the monthly bill jumps after the switch.
- Token counts in your traces (the logged record of each run) are many times higher for the team, while passes rose by only one or two.
- The team passes the same number of tasks as one agent, or fewer, and still costs more.

**Signs the sums themselves went wrong**

- The two designs were run on different task sets, so the numbers can't be compared.
- Failed runs were left out of the bill, which makes both designs look cheaper.
- Traces have no `design` tag, so team and single-agent costs got mixed together.

**Quickest check**

Run both designs on the same tasks. Total each design's full bill, failed runs included. Subtract to get the extra dollars and the extra passes. Divide the dollars by the passes. If one more passed task is worth less to you than that number, keep one agent.

judge.notes: No major problems. The closing check restates the lesson's subtract-and-divide idea in prose, but it gives no code and omits the no-extra-passes case, so it is not a giveaway.

learn:stops.a:
Here are three places where the rule needs extra care.

**Very few test tasks.** With only 10 tasks, "2 more passes" could just be luck. Agents can give different answers each time you run them. Run each design several times, or use a bigger set of tasks, and check that the gap holds up before you trust the cost of each extra pass.

**Tasks that aren't worth the same.** The rule treats every pass as equal. But one extra pass on a high-stakes task, like a refund decision, may be worth far more than ten easy ones. Split your tasks into groups by how much they matter, and work out the cost of each extra pass for each group separately.

**Prices and traffic that change.** Model prices drop, your users ask new kinds of questions, and token use drifts. A team that was too expensive last quarter might be worth it now, or the reverse. Recompute regularly from your traces and the gateway's usage table, rather than deciding once and forgetting it.

learn:term.q: What does “cost per success” mean here?
learn:term.a:
**Cost per success** is the whole bill divided by the number of runs that passed. Failed runs stay in the bill.

**An everyday comparison**

Say you bake 10 cookies and the ingredients cost $5. Two burn. You only eat 8. So each good cookie really cost you $5 ÷ 8, about 63 cents. The burnt ones still used up flour and sugar, so their cost gets spread over the cookies that came out right.

**In the lesson's example**

Both designs ran the same 10 tasks.

- **One agent:** spent $0.50 and passed 6. So $0.50 ÷ 6 is about 8 cents per success.
- **Team:** spent $5.90 and passed 8. So $5.90 ÷ 8 is about $0.74 per success.

Here a "pass" or "success" means a task the agent got right, judged by your evaluation.

**Why the lesson doesn't stop there**

Cost per success tells you what one passed task costs on average. It doesn't tell you what the team's *extra* passes cost. The team's $0.74 looks fairly cheap. But its 2 extra passes cost $2.70 each. That second number is what the rest of the lesson is about.

check:0:0.q: Why not “After about 2 seconds, with the four results it…”?
check:0:0.a:
That option gets one thing right. Four of the five results really are ready after about 2 seconds. And carrying on with "whatever came back in time" is exactly what the lesson recommends.

But it misses the key detail in the question: **there are no timeouts**. The gather step does not start when *most* workers finish. It starts when *every* worker sent out by `Send` has finished. Nothing tells it to stop waiting for the fifth one. So it sits idle for the full 40 seconds, even though four results are already waiting.

Moving on with partial results only happens if you give each worker a timeout. That is what the `asyncio.wait_for(..., timeout=10)` line in the lesson does. When a worker runs past its limit, it stops and adds its name to `late`. Then the gather can run without it. Without that limit, one slow worker holds up the whole run.

"After about 40 seconds, once the slowest worker is done" is better because the gather always waits for the slowest worker unless a timeout cuts it short.

check:0:2.q: Why not “After about 10 seconds, the average time of the…”?
check:0:2.a:
The math in that option is right. Four workers at 2 seconds and one at 40 seconds average out to 9.6 seconds, which is "about 10." It also notices that the slow worker pulls the number up.

But an average answers the wrong question. The gather step does not start when a typical worker is done. It starts when **every** worker is done, because its job is to combine all the results.

The workers run at the same time. So after 2 seconds, four of them are finished and waiting. Their quick times do not speed up the fifth one. The gather sits idle until the 40-second worker comes back.

There are also no timeouts here. A **timeout** is a limit that stops a worker after a set time. Without one, nothing cuts that slow search short. The whole run waits the full 40 seconds.

This is why the lesson gives each worker a timeout.

"After about 40 seconds, once the slowest worker is done" is better because a gather waits for the slowest worker, not the average one.

check:1:0.q: Why not “Only the last write is kept”?
check:1:0.a:
"Only the last write is kept" is a natural guess, and it is half right.

**What it gets right:** a key with no reducer (a rule for combining updates) follows a simple default: each new value replaces the old one. If steps run one after another, the later step's value does win.

**What it misses:** these three workers run at the same time. LangGraph groups work into rounds called "steps," and all three workers finish in the same step. So there is no "last" write. Three values arrive together for one slot, and LangGraph has no rule for picking one.

Rather than quietly keep one and throw two away, it stops and raises an error. That is a kindness. Silently losing two search results would be a bug you might not notice for weeks.

This is why the lesson adds `Annotated[list, operator.add]`. That reducer tells LangGraph to join all three lists instead of choosing between them.

**Why "The run stops with an error" is better:** parallel workers writing the same key with no reducer have no last write to keep, so LangGraph fails loudly instead of guessing.

judge.notes: No real problem. The answer adds a few claims the lesson never states (the default overwrite behaviour, the idea of 'steps'), but they are accurate and do not contradict the lesson.

check:1:1.q: Why not “The lists are joined up anyway”?
check:1:1.a:
**"The lists are joined up anyway"** gets one thing right: joining every worker's list is usually what you *want*. That is the whole point of the gather.

But LangGraph does not join lists on its own. Joining only happens when you attach a **reducer**, the rule for combining updates, such as `operator.add` in `Annotated[list, operator.add]`.

Without a reducer, a key follows the default rule: **replace** the old value with the new one. That works when one step writes the key. Here, three workers write `results` in the same step. LangGraph cannot pick a winner, and it will not guess that you meant "join". So it treats this as a conflict and stops with an error (it raises `InvalidUpdateError`).

That is also a safety feature. A loud error is better than quietly keeping one worker's results and dropping the other two.

**"The run stops with an error"** is better because, with no reducer, LangGraph has no rule for combining three updates to the same key, so it refuses instead of joining them.

judge.notes: Minor: it adds details the lesson never states (the default replace rule and the name InvalidUpdateError). These are accurate and do not contradict the lesson.

check:2:0.q: Why not “Let the fastest worker write first”?
check:2:0.a:
"Let the fastest worker write first" does notice a real problem. Several workers writing to one shared table at the same time can clash. Putting them in an order seems like a fix.

But it misses the main issue. Every worker still changes something outside the graph. That causes a few troubles:

- **The order is random.** Which worker finishes first depends on network speed and load. So the table can end up different on each run.
- **Everyone still writes.** The slow workers write later, but they still write. You still have many writers, just in a different order.
- **Timeouts leave a mess.** If a worker is stopped at 10 seconds partway through saving, you may get half-written notes.
- **Retries make copies.** If the run is repeated, every worker saves again, and you get duplicate rows.

This is why the lesson keeps workers **read-only**. They only search and hand back results. They never touch the table.

"Workers only search; one later step saves" is better because a single step, running after the gather has everything, does all the writing once and in one place.

judge.notes: No real problems; the half-written notes and duplicate-row points go slightly beyond the lesson but do not contradict it.

check:2:2.q: Why not “Each worker writes to its own table copy”?
check:2:2.a:
This option does get one thing right. If every worker has its own copy of the table, no two workers write to the same place at once. So they won't clash or overwrite each other's notes.

But it misses the lesson's main rule: keep the workers **read-only**. Read-only means a worker only looks things up. It changes nothing outside the graph. With table copies, every worker is still saving data outside the graph. You haven't removed the risky writes. You've just spread them across more tables.

It also adds work. The copies are separate, so something still has to combine them into one table later.

The lesson's design avoids all of this. Each worker just returns what it found. A **reducer**, a rule for combining updates, joins those results into one list. Here that rule is `operator.add`. Next comes the **gather**, the step that collects every worker's results in one place. After the gather, a single step does all the saving.

"Workers only search; one later step saves" is better because all writing happens once, in one place, after every result has been collected.

explain:gotcha.q: Why does “Give a shared key a reducer” matter?
explain:gotcha.a:
When you fan out with `Send`, all the workers finish in the same step. Each one hands back an update for the shared state, like `{"found": [result]}`.

If `found` is a plain key, LangGraph sees several workers trying to set the same value at once. It can't tell which one should win. So it stops the whole run with `InvalidUpdateError`, its error for "conflicting writes to one key."

A **reducer** is a rule that tells LangGraph how to combine those writes. With `Annotated[list, operator.add]`, it joins the lists together instead of picking one.

A small example: you search wiki and tickets.

- **Plain key:** both workers write `found` in the same step. The run crashes. You get no results, even though both searches worked.
- **With the reducer:** `found` becomes `[wiki_result, tickets_result]`, and the gather step sees both.

This catches people in real work because a test with one source passes. There is only one write, so nothing clashes. Then a real run with five sources fails.

```python
found: list                            # plain: crashes on 2+ writes
found: Annotated[list, operator.add]   # joins every worker's list
```

learn:spot.q: How would I spot it going wrong?
learn:spot.a:
**Warning signs to watch for**

- **The run is as slow as its slowest search.** One source takes 30 seconds, so every run takes 30 seconds, or sometimes never finishes. That means a worker has no timeout. A timeout is a time limit after which you stop waiting.
- **The run crashes with an error about one key getting several updates.** The `found` list is missing its reducer. A reducer is the rule that joins every worker's list into one.
- **One slow source stops the whole run.** The timeout was put on the graph step itself. A graph step is called a node. That kind of timeout ends everything unless the node also has an error handler, which is a fallback that catches the failure and carries on.
- **A source quietly goes missing.** It is not in the results, and the timed-out list is empty too.

**Quickest check**

Make one source slow on purpose, say 30 seconds. Then open the trace, which is a step-by-step record of the run with timings. All searches should start together. The gather should begin at your time limit, not at 30 seconds. The slow source should be named in the timed-out list.

learn:stops.a:
**1. The parts depend on each other.** Fan-out only works when each part can run without the others. If one search needs another's result first, running them at the same time gives wrong or empty answers. Run those steps in order, and fan out only the parts that are truly independent.

**2. A missing result changes the answer.** Carrying on without a late worker is fine when the sources are "nice to have." If billing data is essential, a reply without it can mislead. Retry the late worker, or tell the user plainly that the answer is incomplete.

**3. You fan out to hundreds of workers.** Many calls at once can hit **rate limits** (a service's cap on requests per minute) and run up cost. Limit how many workers run at the same time, for example in batches of ten. Also keep timeouts short so the slowest batch doesn't drag on.

A related trap: if a worker writes something, like sending an email, a timeout won't undo it. That is why the writing belongs in one step after the gather.

judge.notes: No significant problems: the three situations are sensible extensions of the lesson, about 180 words, with no code and no exercise solution.

learn:term.a:
Fan-out and gather are two halves of one pattern.

**Fan-out** is the splitting step. One job becomes several independent parts, and each part goes to its own worker. In LangGraph, `Send` starts one worker per part. The workers run at the same time.

**Gather** (also called fan-in) is the combining step. It collects every worker's result in one place. A reducer (a rule for combining updates), here `operator.add`, joins each worker's list into one shared list, so the workers don't clash.

The key difference is direction. Fan-out spreads work outward, and gather pulls results back in. Fan-out just hands out the work. Gather has to wait, because it can't start until the slowest worker finishes or is stopped.

Think of dinner with friends. Inviting five friends is the fan-out. Waiting at the table is the gather. You only wait until a set time, then order with whoever arrived.

In the lesson's example, three searches fan out. Wiki returns at 2 seconds and tickets at 4. Billing would take 30, but the 10-second timeout stops it. So the gather runs at 10 seconds with wiki and tickets, and lists billing as timed out.

check:0:0.q: Why not “Add one more helper that looks up the order num…”?
check:0:0.a:
The trace already shows the research helper found the order number. So finding it was never the problem. The number got lost later, in the **hand-off**, the moment the helper passed its work to the main agent.

"Add one more helper that looks up the order number again" does get one thing right. It aims at the exact fact that keeps going missing.

But it fixes the wrong step. The new helper would also hand its work to the main agent. If the main agent still retells messages in its own words, the number can drop out again. You would have one more hand-off, so one more place to lose details. You would also pay for an extra agent run and wait longer for each answer.

It also only covers the order number. Next week it might be a date or a card ending, and you would need yet another helper.

"Have helpers report every finding, passed on word for word" is better because it fixes the hand-off itself, so every fact the helpers find, not just the order number, reaches the final answer.

check:0:1.q: Why not “Give the main agent a bigger model, so it remem…”?
check:0:1.a:
It sounds sensible, but it aims at the wrong problem.

**What it gets partly right:** a stronger model might reword a bit more carefully. So it could help a little, sometimes.

**What it misses:** the trace (the step-by-step record of what each agent did) shows the helper *found* the order number. So nothing was forgotten from lack of memory. The fact got lost at the **hand-off**, the moment the helper passed its work on.

That can happen in two ways:

- The helper's final message left the fact out. The main agent sees only that final message. No model, however big, can keep a fact it was never shown.
- The main agent retold the message in its own words and dropped the detail. Bigger models reword too, so the leak stays.

A bigger model also costs more on every run, and it doesn't touch either cause.

**Why the other option is better:** having helpers put every finding in their final message, and passing it on word for word, fixes the exact spot where the fact falls out, cheaply, through the prompts.

judge.notes: No real problems. The cost remark and the claim that bigger models still reword go slightly beyond the lesson but do not contradict it.

check:1:0.q: Why not “The helpers have to run all over again”?
check:1:0.a:
Rewording doesn't make the helpers run again. Each helper has already finished and sent its **final message** (the last thing it says when its work is done). The main agent just takes that message and retells it in its own words. Nothing in that step sends the work back to the helpers.

This option does get one thing right. It senses that something goes wrong at the **hand-off**, the moment one agent passes its work to another. That is the right place to look.

But it picks the wrong problem. A rerun would be easy to spot, since it costs time and you'd see extra helper steps in the trace (the record of every step a run took). The real risk is quiet. The answer still reads well, so nobody notices that a detail fell out during the retelling. That is why the lesson says to check which facts reach the final answer word for word.

"A key fact, like a refund date, drops out" is better because it names the real danger: rewording silently loses a detail that mattered, even though the answer still sounds fine.

judge.notes: No real problems; the only weak spot is the claim that a rerun would show up as extra helper steps in the trace, which the lesson doesn't state, though it doesn't contradict the lesson either.

check:1:2.q: Why not “The answers become far too long to read”?
check:1:2.a:
"The answers become far too long to read" points at the wrong problem. It worries about length, and length is easy to spot. You would notice a long, rambling answer just by reading it.

The question already tells you the answers read well. So readability is not where the danger lies.

The lesson's worry is quieter. When the main agent retells a helper's report in its own words, details can fall out. Think of a message passed from person to person, each time in new words. The answer still sounds smooth and complete, but one fact that mattered is gone. In the lesson's example, "card ends 0099" never reaches the final answer, and nothing about the answer looks wrong.

That is why the lesson suggests a **hand-off check** (testing the moment one agent passes its work to another). You list the helper's facts and see which ones appear word for word in the final answer.

"A key fact, like a refund date, drops out" is better because it names the real, hidden risk: an answer that reads well but has silently lost information.

judge.notes: No significant problems; the point that long answers are easy to spot goes slightly beyond the lesson but does not contradict it.

check:2:0.a:
"Allow longer final answers" has a fair instinct behind it. If facts are going missing, more room might seem to let more of them fit.

But length isn't what's losing them. The facts fall out at the **hand-off**, the moment a helper passes its work to the main agent. The main agent rewords the helper's message, and details drop out along the way. A longer answer can still be reworded. It can be padded with friendly filler while the order number or card digits still go missing.

There's a second problem. Your grader already says the answers look good. So making them longer gives you no new way to *see* the loss. You'd be guessing whether it helped. You still wouldn't know which facts vanish, or how often.

The real fix lives in the prompts. Helpers put every finding in their final message, and the main agent passes it on word for word. A check then tells you whether that fix worked.

"Check which found facts reach the answer" is better because it measures the exact spot where information leaks. It also names what was lost, so you know what to fix.

judge.notes: No real problems. The closing explanation runs to two sentences where one was asked for, and the text sits just under the 200-word limit.

check:2:1.q: Why not “Grade writing style more strictly”?
check:2:1.a:
"Grade writing style more strictly" sounds sensible, but it aims at the wrong problem.

**What it gets right:** grading the final answer is a good first step. The lesson says to do that first. Style also matters to users a little.

**What it misses:** the answers already score well. They read smoothly. The complaint is that facts are missing, not that the writing is poor. A style grader looks at how the answer sounds, not at what the helpers found. So it can't notice that "card ends 0099" never arrived.

It could even make things worse. A stricter style grader may reward polished rewording. Rewording is exactly how details fall out during the hand-off (the moment one agent passes its work to another). And even if it lowered a score, it wouldn't tell you *which* fact was lost or *where* it went missing.

**Why "Check which found facts reach the answer" is better:** it compares the helper's list of facts with the final answer word for word, so it measures what users are actually complaining about and names the exact facts that were dropped.

judge.notes: No blocking problems. The claims that style matters 'a little' and that a stricter style grader 'may reward polished rewording' go beyond the lesson, but they are hedged and do not contradict it.

explain:gotcha.q: Why does “Pass findings on word for word” matter?
explain:gotcha.a:
The main agent never sees what a helper did along the way. It sees only the helper's final message. So that message is the only bridge between the two.

When the main agent retells that message in its own words, it tends to keep the gist and drop the exact details. The trouble is that the exact details are often what the user needs.

Here is a small example. A support team has a researcher helper. It finds three things:

- order 4412
- refund approved
- card ends 0099

The main agent rewrites this as: "Good news, your refund was approved and is on its way."

That reads well. But the order number and the card are gone. The customer can't tell which order it was, or which card the money goes back to. Nobody notices, because nothing looks broken.

The fix lives in the prompts (the instructions you give each agent):

- Helpers put every finding in their final message.
- The main agent passes those findings on word for word.

In LangChain's tests, this was one of three fixes that together made answers nearly 50 percent better.

learn:spot.q: How would I spot it going wrong?
learn:spot.a:
**Warning signs the hand-off is losing facts**

- **The final-answer grade looks fine, but users complain.** Answers read smoothly, yet people ask "which order?" or "what card?" The polish hides the missing detail.
- **Vague words replace exact ones.** The answer says "your order" or "your card" where the helper had "order 4412" or "card ends 0099." That is the main agent rewording instead of passing facts on word for word.
- **Your hand-off score is well below 1.0.** The lost list keeps naming the same kind of fact, such as numbers, dates or IDs.

**Signs the check itself is broken**

- **It always returns 1.0.** The helper's span (one recorded step in the trace) may have no `facts` in its outputs. So nothing gets checked.
- **Facts show as lost when they are plainly there.** Small changes like "#4412" versus "4412" can cause a miss.

**Quickest check**

Open one trace in MLflow. Put the `researcher` span's outputs beside the final answer. Tick off each fact by hand. Then compare your count with the score.

learn:stops.a:
**When a fact is reworded on purpose**, like "card ending in 0099" instead of "card ends 0099", the check marks it lost even though it arrived. For facts like that, match a short core piece such as "0099", or use an LLM judge (a model asked to grade meaning, not exact words).

**When a short fact hides inside longer text**, the `in` check can be fooled. The fact "12" is found inside "4412", so it counts as kept when it never really arrived. Use longer, distinctive facts, or match whole words only.

**When some facts should be left out**, a low share is not a failure. A helper's side notes, or private details like a full card number, often shouldn't reach the user. List only the facts the user truly needs, and score the hand-off on those.

learn:term.a:
A **hand-off** is the moment one agent passes its work to another.

Think of a relay race. One runner finishes their leg and hands the baton to the next runner. If the baton slips during that pass, it doesn't matter how fast either runner was. Something got dropped in between.

Or think of a shift change at a hospital. The night nurse tells the day nurse what happened overnight. If the night nurse sums it up loosely, one key detail can go missing, even though the summary sounds fine.

In this lesson, the runners are agents. A helper agent (here, the `researcher`) does some digging. Then it passes its **final message** to the main agent. That pass is the hand-off. The main agent only sees that message, nothing else the helper did.

In the example, the researcher found three facts: `order 4412`, `refund approved`, and `card ends 0099`. The final answer kept the first two but dropped the card number. So the hand-off kept 2 of 3 facts, about 0.67. The lost fact was `card ends 0099`.

check:0:1.q: Why not “Add a second agent, so each agent owns one of t…”?
check:0:1.a:
The idea has one thing right. If each agent holds only one of the two tools, neither agent can mix them up on its own.

But the confusion doesn't go away. It moves up a level. Now a main agent has to choose which helper to call. If the two helpers sound alike, it makes the same mistake. You also pay for it. A team uses several times more **tokens** (the pieces of text a model reads and writes, which you pay for).

Two more signs point away from a team. First, one agent already passes 70 percent. That is well above the rough 45 percent hint, and past that point more agents helped little or made things worse. Second, this job doesn't split into **independent parts** (pieces separate people could do without talking). It is one job with a naming problem.

So the lesson's rule applies: fix the first agent's tools before adding a second.

"Rename and describe the two tools clearly, then rerun the eval" is better because it fixes the actual cause cheaply, and the rerun shows you whether it worked.

check:0:2.q: Why not “Move to a bigger model, so it can tell the two …”?
check:0:2.a:
A bigger model isn't crazy. Larger models often reason better, so it *might* confuse the two tools less often. That part is fair.

But it misses where the problem comes from. The model only knows a tool by its name and its description (the short text that says what the tool does). If two tools are called `get_order` and `get_orders` with vague descriptions, even a strong model has to guess. The confusing labels are still there. You've just paid for a better guesser.

A bigger model also costs more on every call and is often slower. And you haven't fixed anything you can point to.

The lesson's rule is to fix the first agent's tool names and descriptions before reaching for something heavier. You already named the problem: two similar tools. So fix exactly that. Then rerun your eval (your fixed set of test tasks with a score) to see whether the misses went away.

"Rename and describe the two tools clearly, then rerun the eval" is better because it fixes the actual cause cheaply and then checks the result, instead of spending more money hoping the model guesses better.

judge.notes: No major problems. It says what a bigger model gets right, what it misses, and why renaming and re-running the eval is better. It is close to the length limit, and it stretches the lesson's 'before adding a second agent' rule into 'before something heavier'.

check:1:1.a:
"One agent with tools" is a fair guess. An agent could do this job. You would give it three tools, say `read_form`, `check_form` and `file_form`, and it would probably call them in the right order.

But "probably" is the problem. With an agent, the model picks which tool to call and when. That freedom helps when the next step depends on what just happened, like deciding whether a refund is needed. Here nothing needs deciding. The steps are always the same three, in the same order.

So the agent adds cost and risk for no gain:

- **More tokens.** The model spends a call deciding each next step, even though the answer never changes.
- **Room for mistakes.** It might skip the check, repeat a step, or file before checking.
- **Harder to test.** Its path can differ from run to run, so your evals have more to cover.

The ladder says to climb only for a problem you can name. This task gives you no such problem.

A fixed workflow is better because your code locks in the order once, so every form gets read, checked and filed the same way, every time.

judge.notes: No real problems; the token, mistake and testing points go slightly beyond the lesson's text but do not contradict it.

check:1:2.a:
"A team of agents" gets one thing right: the job really does have three separate steps. It's natural to picture one agent per step.

But a team fits work that splits into **independent parts**. Those are pieces you could hand to people who never talk to each other. These steps aren't like that. You can't check a form before it's read, and you can't file it before it's checked. Each step needs the one before it.

The order also never changes. So nobody has to decide what happens next. Agents earn their place when a model needs to choose which tool to call, and when. Here there's no choice to make.

A team would still cost you. It uses several times more tokens (the chunks of text you pay the model to read and write). It also has more moving parts to debug. In the large study the lesson mentions, every team design did worse on step-by-step tasks like this one.

"A fixed workflow" is better because your code runs the same three steps in the same order every time, which is exactly what this task needs.

check:2:0.q: Why not “Go back to a single model call”?
check:2:0.a:
"Go back to a single model call" gets one thing right. The lesson does say to pick the lowest step on the ladder that does the job. Preferring simple designs is a good habit.

But the ladder also says to climb a step when you can name a problem. Here you can name one, and it has two parts:

- The job splits into five **independent parts**. These are pieces you could hand to people who never talk to each other.
- One agent passes only 30 percent of your eval. That is below the rough 45 percent hint from the study.

Those are exactly the signs the lesson gives for trying a team. Stepping down the ladder doesn't answer them. Nothing in the question suggests the work is simple enough for one call. Going lower just ignores the problem you found.

"Try a team, and check it on your eval" is better because it matches the named problem (independent parts and a low pass rate) and still makes you measure whether the team actually helps.

check:2:2.q: Why not “Give the one agent a longer prompt”?
check:2:2.a:
"Give the one agent a longer prompt" gets one thing right. It stays low on the ladder. Staying low is the lesson's default, since a team uses several times more tokens (the chunks of text a model reads and writes, which you pay for).

But it misses what this job is telling you. The research splits into five parts that never need each other. Those are **independent parts**: pieces you could hand to people who never talk. That is exactly the shape the lesson says a team fits. A longer prompt doesn't use that shape. It still leaves one agent doing all five parts by itself.

The pass rate matters too. The lesson's rough hint is that once one agent passes about 45 percent, more agents helped little or made things worse. Here one agent passes 30 percent, below that line, so the hint doesn't warn you off a team. It doesn't promise a team will win either. That's why you measure.

"Try a team, and check it on your eval" is better because it matches the job's independent parts, and it makes you prove the extra cost pays off.

explain:gotcha.q: Why does “Use the simplest design that works” matter?
explain:gotcha.a:
Every step up the ladder costs something, even when the higher step seems to work.

A fixed workflow runs the same steps in the same order every time. You can test each step on its own. When something breaks, you know where to look.

An agent picks its own tools while it runs. That freedom helps when the path really changes from job to job. When it doesn't, you pay anyway: more model calls, more tokens (the chunks of text you're billed for), slower replies, and runs that differ for no reason.

A small example. Every support ticket gets tagged, routed, then answered. Someone builds an agent for it. Most days it works. Some days it skips tagging, or routes the ticket twice. Each run costs several extra calls. When a ticket lands with the wrong team, nobody can say why, because the agent chose its own path.

The same three steps as a `StateGraph` with fixed edges would never skip a step. It would also be easy to test.

So start low on the ladder. Climb only when you can name the problem the next step solves.

judge.notes: No significant problems: the answer matches the lesson, stays under 200 words, and gives no exercise solution. The invented ticket example is reasonable, and `StateGraph` is only lightly explained.

learn:spot.q: How would I spot it going wrong?
learn:spot.a:
Here are the signs that a team was added when it wasn't needed.

**Your token bill jumps.** Tokens are the chunks of text a model reads and writes, and you pay per token. The lesson says teams use several times more. If cost multiplies but your eval score barely moves, that's a red flag. (An eval is your set of test tasks with a pass rate.)

**Step-by-step tasks get worse.** In the study, every team design did worse on tasks where each step depends on the one before. If your agents keep passing half-finished work back and forth, the parts aren't truly **independent**. Those are pieces that people who never talk could each do alone.

**One agent was already doing well.** If one agent passed about 45 percent or more, extra agents tend to help little or hurt.

**Quickest check:** go back to one agent. Fix its tool names and descriptions so the model can tell which tool does what. Rerun your evals. Then compare pass rate and token use with the team's. If the single agent comes close, drop back down the ladder.

learn:stops.a:
Here are three situations where the ladder rule needs extra care.

**Your model or tasks differ from the study.** The 45 percent line came from one study, with its own models and tasks. A newer model, or a very different kind of job, can move that line. Treat 0.45 as a starting guess, and test both designs on your own eval (your set of test tasks with known good answers).

**The parts only look independent.** Six vendor reports seem separate, but they may need to agree, for example by using the same scoring scale or not repeating each other. Helper agents that never talk will drift apart. Use one agent, or a workflow that passes each result to the next step.

**Your eval is tiny.** With only ten test tasks, one lucky or unlucky answer moves the pass rate by 10 percent. So 30 versus 45 percent might just be noise. Add more test tasks first, then decide whether to climb the ladder.

learn:term.a:
In this lesson they mean the **same thing**. "Team" is just the short, friendly name. "Multi-agent system" is the formal term you'll see in papers and docs.

Both describe several agents that split up the work. An **agent** here is a model that can decide which tool to call, and when. A team has more than one of these, and each one handles part of the job.

The only difference is the setting where you'd use each word. Think of "car" and "motor vehicle." Same object. You say "car" to a friend. A legal form says "motor vehicle." The lesson says "team" to keep things readable and names the formal term once so you'll recognise it later.

Take the lesson's example: researching 6 vendors, each on its own. A team, or a multi-agent system, could give each vendor to a separate helper agent. A main agent would then combine their findings. Whatever you call it, the warning is the same. It uses several times more tokens, so only try it when the work splits into independent parts. Then measure whether it actually helped.

judge.notes: Minor: the claims about why the lesson uses each word, and where you'd see the formal term, go slightly beyond the lesson, but nothing contradicts it.

check:0:0.q: Why not “Let both write, and keep whichever update lands…”?
check:0:0.a:
"Keep whichever update lands last" sounds fair, but it is really a description of the problem, not a fix.

**What it gets right:** something always gets saved. Nothing crashes, and it is simple to set up.

**What it misses:** the earlier change is thrown away without anyone noticing. Say one helper adds the tag `refund` and the other adds `urgent`. If the `urgent` save lands last, `refund` is gone. No error, no warning. That silent overwrite is exactly the **lost update** the lesson warns about.

It also leaves the outcome to timing. Which save lands last depends on which helper happens to finish second. So you can't tell in advance whose work will survive.

**Why "Have both report back, and let one agent write the tags" is better:** with one writer (the **single-writer** rule), both reports reach a single agent. That agent can combine them into one set of tags. Then no helper's change gets quietly wiped out by another's.

judge.notes: Minor: the 'better' explanation runs three sentences instead of the one requested, but the content is accurate and consistent with the lesson.

check:0:1.q: Why not “Run them one after the other, so they never ove…”?
check:0:1.a:
**Why not "Run them one after the other"?**

This option gets one thing right. If the two helpers never run at the same time, they can't both be changing the tags at the same moment.

But it misses two things.

First, it ignores the question. The question says the helpers *must* run side by side. Running them one after the other breaks that requirement instead of solving the problem.

Second, it only changes *when* they write, not *who* writes. There are still two writers of the tags. The second helper can still save its own tags and replace the first helper's work. That quiet replacing is the **lost update** the lesson warns about. Taking turns doesn't stop it. It only avoids a collision in time.

The lesson's fix is the **single-writer** rule: each thing that changes gets one writer. Helpers only read and report back.

**Why "Have both report back, and let one agent write the tags" is better:** both helpers can still run side by side, and since only one agent ever saves the tags, nothing gets quietly overwritten.

check:1:1.q: Why not “By adding a fourth agent to check”?
check:1:1.a:
Adding a checker agent sounds sensible. It gets one thing right: reviewing work can catch mistakes, and catching mistakes matters.

But it doesn't fix why details go missing. In a planner, coder and tester setup, details are lost at each **hand-off**, the moment one agent passes its work to the next. Each hand-off is a summary, and summaries drop things. It's like a message passed from person to person, changing a little each time.

A fourth agent adds one more hand-off, not one fewer. The checker only sees what reached it. If a detail was dropped between the planner and the coder, the checker never had it, so it can't put it back. At best, it notices something looks wrong after the damage is done.

So the checker treats the symptom, the missing details, without touching the cause, which is the way the work was split.

"By what each agent needs to know" is better because each agent gets the full context its piece needs from the start, so there's less to lose at each hand-off.

check:1:2.q: Why not “By giving each agent more tools”?
check:1:2.a:
"More tools" sounds helpful, but it doesn't touch the real problem.

**What it gets right:** tools do matter. A helper's brief (its short set of instructions) names which tools to use. A read-only tool like `read_invoices` is how the billing helper gets the facts it needs.

**What it misses:** the details go missing at the hand-offs. A hand-off is the moment one agent passes its work to the next. In the planner → coder → tester setup, each agent passes a summary to the next one, and a little gets lost each time. Giving every agent extra tools keeps those same job-title boundaries. So the same hand-offs still happen, and details still slip through them. More tools also doesn't settle who writes what, so two agents could still change the same thing.

The fix is about *where you draw the lines* between agents, not how much each one is equipped with.

**Why "By what each agent needs to know" is better:** it draws each agent's boundary around the context its piece of work needs, so fewer details have to survive a hand-off at all.

check:2:0.q: Why not “A bigger model for each helper”?
check:2:0.a:
A bigger model is a reasonable thought. A stronger model often follows instructions better and reasons more carefully. So it's not a silly guess.

But it misses the real problem. The brief just says "look into refunds." That tells each helper almost nothing about where its job starts and stops. A smarter model still can't read your mind. It also can't see what the other helper was told. So both helpers sensibly decide "look into refunds" means "run a search," and you get the same work done twice.

A bigger model also costs more and runs slower. You'd pay extra and still get the overlap.

The fix belongs in the brief, not the model. Think of two new coworkers given the same vague sticky note. Hiring smarter coworkers doesn't help. Telling each one exactly what to cover does.

"A clear goal and what's out of scope" is the right answer because it gives each helper a fenced-off piece of work, so no two helpers wander into the same search.

check:2:2.q: Why not “More tools for each helper”?
check:2:2.a:
"More tools for each helper" sounds helpful, but it doesn't touch the cause.

The problem in the question is the brief. A **brief** is the short instruction a helper gets before it starts. "Look into refunds" is vague. It doesn't say what the helper should find, or where its job stops. So two helpers can each decide the same search is their job, and both run it. That's duplicated work.

Tools are the actions a helper can take, like reading invoices. Giving each helper more of them changes *what it can do*. It doesn't tell it *what it should do*. A vague brief plus extra tools still leaves the helpers guessing about their piece. It may even give them more room to drift into each other's work.

The lesson does say a brief should name which tools to use. But that's one part of a good brief, not a fix for a missing goal and scope.

The better answer is "A clear goal and what's out of scope." It tells each helper exactly which piece is theirs and which piece belongs to someone else, so they stop repeating each other's work.

explain:gotcha.a:
When two helpers save the same thing, neither knows about the other. Each reads the current value, makes its change, and saves its own full version. The last save wins. The earlier change disappears, with no error or warning. This is a **lost update**.

**Example:** a ticket's tags start as `["new"]`. The `triage` helper reads them and adds `"urgent"`. At the same time, the `billing` helper reads `["new"]` and adds `"refund"`. Triage saves `["new", "urgent"]`. Then billing saves `["new", "refund"]`. The "urgent" tag is gone. The `reply` helper then drafts a slow, routine answer to an angry customer.

In real work, this hurts because nothing crashes. The logs look normal. The bug only appears when the timing lines up a certain way, so it is hard to reproduce and track down.

**The fix:** `billing` doesn't save tags. It reports "add a refund tag" back instead. Only one node, the single writer, saves tags. It sees every suggestion and combines them. Sharing what you *read* is fine. Only saving needs one owner.

learn:spot.q: How would I spot it going wrong?
learn:spot.a:
**Warning signs the split went wrong**

- **Things change for no clear reason.** A ticket's tags were right a moment ago, then they change or vanish. Usually two helpers wrote to the same thing, and the later one quietly replaced the earlier one. That is a **lost update**.
- **It works in testing, then breaks in real use.** With one ticket at a time, writes rarely collide. Under real load, helpers run close together and start overwriting each other.
- **Results differ between runs.** Same input, different final tags. Whichever helper finished last "won."
- **Repeated work in the traces.** A **trace** is the step-by-step record of what each agent did. If two helpers look up the same invoices, their briefs were too vague.
- **Details fade at each hand-off.** A fact present early is missing or changed by the final answer. That points to splitting by job title instead of by what each agent needs to know.

**Quickest check**

Open one trace. List every tool call that *changes* something, such as `save_tags`. Next to each, note which agent made it. Any resource with more than one agent writing to it is your problem.

learn:stops.a:
Here are three places where this rule needs extra care.

**The one writer gets overloaded.** If every helper reports to a single main agent, that agent's context (everything it has read so far) fills up and it slows down. Instead, split the shared thing into parts, like one writer per customer or per table. Each part still has exactly one writer.

**Hidden writes.** Counting writers only works if the `writes` lists are honest. A "read-only" helper whose tool can still update a database is a second writer nobody counted. Check what each tool can actually do, and give helpers access keys that only allow reading.

**Data changes while helpers work.** A helper reads invoices and reports back. Before the writer saves, someone edits an invoice, so the report is stale (out of date). Have the writer re-check key facts right before saving, or ask helpers to say when they read the data.

learn:term.a:
They're the same idea, just phrased two ways. The lesson treats them as one concept.

**"One writer"** is the plain description. Each thing that changes (the final answer, a table, a file) has exactly one agent allowed to change it.

**"Single-writer"** is the name of the rule that requires this. You'll hear it as "the single-writer rule" in docs and interviews.

So the only difference is that one describes the setup and the other names the rule. They work together like this: the rule says "keep it this way," and checking for one writer is how you confirm you followed it.

**Everyday comparison:** a shared shopping list on the fridge. Everyone can read it, but only one person edits it. Others tell that person what to add. If two people edit at once, one person's change can quietly vanish. That's a **lost update**.

**The lesson's example:** `"tags"` is written by both `triage` and `billing`. That breaks the rule. The fix is for `billing` to report to `triage`, so `triage` is the one writer of `"tags"`. Reading is still fine for anyone.

judge.notes: No significant problems; the only small extra is that "in docs" goes slightly beyond the lesson, but it doesn't contradict it.

check:0:0.q: Why not “Twenty questions is too few to compare any two …”?
check:0:0.a:
"Twenty questions is too few" points at something real. With a small set, a gap of 2 passes is thin evidence. More questions would make the comparison steadier.

But it misses the main problem in this setup. Each design ran only **once**. Agents give different answers on different tries, so the same agent might pass 12 today and 14 tomorrow. A gap of 2 could be that wobble, not a real difference between the designs.

It also goes too far. "Too few to compare **any** two designs" says 20 questions can never be used. The lesson's own example still uses 20 questions. What it adds is 3 tries per question. A question counts as **passed every time** only if every try passed. Repeating each question like that is what deals with lucky single tries.

So more questions might help a bit. The bigger missing piece here is more tries per question.

"One run each: agents vary, so 2 more passes may be luck" is better because it names the actual flaw, a single try per design, and points straight to the fix: run each question 3 to 5 times.

check:0:2.q: Why not “The team should have been run on harder questio…”?
check:0:2.a:
That option has a fair point. The questions you test on do matter. If every question is easy, both designs pass, and you learn little. So it's reasonable to want questions that can tell the designs apart.

But it misses the real problem. Each design ran **once** per question. Agents give different answers on different tries. So a gap of 2 passes in 20 could just be luck. Run again, and one agent might score 14 while the team scores 12.

Harder questions don't fix that. With one try each, results on hard questions would be just as shaky. You still couldn't tell skill from luck.

There's a second catch. Testing only on hard questions skews the test away from the mix of questions the agent will really face. Swapping the question set after seeing results is also a quiet way to bend the experiment. That's the same thing a decision rule written ahead of time is meant to stop.

"One run each: agents vary, so 2 more passes may be luck" is the better answer. It names the actual flaw: too few tries to trust a small gap. That's why the lesson runs each question 3 to 5 times.

judge.notes: Passes all checks; the 'skews away from real questions' point goes beyond the lesson and the answer loosely links swapping questions to the decision rule, but neither contradicts it.

check:1:1.q: Why not “A gain that small is too hard to measure”?
check:1:1.a:
That option points at a real worry, but not the one in the question.

**What it gets right:** small gains are hard to trust. Agents give different answers on different tries. With only 20 questions, one question is 0.05 of the score, so a bit of luck can move the result. That's why the lesson runs each question 3 to 5 times.

**What it misses:** nobody in the question is saying the gain can't be measured. The team was measured and fell short. The problem is what happens next: someone wants to lower the bar *because they saw the result*. Also, if a small gain really were too noisy to trust, the fix would be more questions or more tries. Lowering the bar would make it easier to call a weak result a win.

The **decision rule** is written before any run so the result can't choose the rule. Changing it afterward undoes that protection.

**Why "It moves the goalposts after the result" is better:** it names the actual mistake, which is changing the rule after seeing the outcome so that a loss gets relabeled as a win.

check:1:2.q: Why not “The rule should only be about cost”?
check:1:2.a:
"The rule should only be about cost" is not the best answer, because it doesn't deal with what went wrong.

It gets one thing right. Cost matters, and the lesson's rule does include a cost limit of 50 cents per success. (Cost per success means total cost divided by the number of passed tries.)

But it misses two things.

First, it drops quality. A cost-only rule asks "is it cheap enough?" and never asks "does it pass more questions?" In the example, the team's $0.35 is under the 50-cent limit. So a cost-only rule would accept the team even if it passed fewer questions than one agent. That defeats the point of the experiment, which is to find out whether the team does better.

Second, it skips the real problem. Someone saw the result and wants to change the rule to fit it. Swapping in a cost-only rule at that moment is still changing the rule after the fact. It is just a different change.

"It moves the goalposts after the result" is better because it names the actual mistake: the rule was written before any run so that no result could rewrite it, and editing it now breaks that promise.

check:2:0.q: Why not “How many tries each question needs”?
check:2:0.a:
That option mixes up two different parts of the experiment.

**What it gets right:** tries do matter here. Agents give different answers on different tries, so you run each question 3 to 5 times. A question counts as "passed every time" only if every try passed.

**What it misses:** you pick the number of tries before any run, and every design gets the same number. In the example, all three designs get 3 tries per question. So the third design can't tell you how many tries to use. That choice is already made.

The third design is an **ablation**. That means taking one part out to see what changes. Here the part is the checker. The two team designs differ only in the checker, so any gap between them comes from it.

Look at the example. The team passes every time on 15 of 20 questions. The team without its checker passes on 12 of 20, the same as one agent. The whole gain disappears when the checker goes.

"What the checker adds to the team" is better because comparing the two teams isolates the checker's effect, and that is exactly what an ablation measures.

check:2:1.q: Why not “Whether the team beats one agent”?
check:2:1.a:
"Whether the team beats one agent" is a real question this experiment answers. But the third design isn't what answers it.

That question comes from comparing the full team to the **baseline** (the one agent, the design you compare against). In the example, the team passed every time on 15 of 20 questions and the one agent on 12 of 20. You would get that answer even without a third design.

The third design, the team without its checker, does a different job. It is an **ablation**: you take one part out and see what changes. Only one thing differs between the two teams, which is the checker. So any gap between them is down to the checker.

In the example, the team without its checker drops to 12 of 20. That is no better than the one agent. So the checker is what makes the team win. Without it, the extra agents add cost but no gain.

"What the checker adds to the team" is the better answer because the third design differs from the full team only by its checker, so it measures that one part.

explain:gotcha.q: Why does “Run each design several times” matter?
explain:gotcha.a:
Agents don't give the same answer every time. Ask the same question twice, and one try may pass while the next fails. So any single run is partly luck.

Here's what goes wrong when you ignore that. Say you run each design once on 20 questions. The team passes 14 and one agent passes 12. That looks like a gain of 1 in 10, so you switch to the team. Later you find that the team's 2 extra passes were lucky tries. Now you pay more per success for a team that isn't actually more reliable.

Running each question 3 to 5 times helps. A question counts as "passed every time" only if every try passed. A question the team got right only by luck will often fail on a later try, so it stops counting as a pass. Repeats can't remove luck completely. A lucky question can still pass every try. But they make a lucky gain much less likely to look real.

This is separate from the decision rule. What keeps the rule honest is writing it down before any run.

learn:spot.q: How would I spot it going wrong?
learn:spot.a:
Here are the signs that the experiment was skipped or done badly.

**The rule moved.** The required gain matches the result too neatly. For example, the rule asks for 0.15 and the team got exactly 0.15. That hints the rule was written after the numbers came in.

**Only one try per question.** Each question has a single trace (one recorded run) per design. Scores look great, then drop in real use. That happens because one lucky try counted as "passed every time."

**Unequal questions.** One design answered 20 questions and another answered 18. Then the comparison isn't fair.

**Rerun flips the winner.** You run it again and the team loses. The first win was probably luck.

**No ablation.** You have no "team, no checker" design. So nobody can say which part earns the extra cost.

**Cost looks oddly cheap.** Cost may have been divided by all tries, not just the passed ones.

**Quickest check:** In MLflow, open each design's traces. Confirm three things:

- Every design has the same questions.
- Each question has 3 to 5 tries.
- The written rule is dated before the first run.

judge.notes: No major problem. The 'rule moved' example (0.15 matching exactly) is a weak signal, and the rule's date would not be in the MLflow traces, but neither contradicts the lesson.

learn:stops.a:
Here are three situations where the rule needs extra care.

**Very few questions.** With only 20 questions, one question that passes by luck moves the score by 0.05. That can tip the verdict all on its own. Use more questions, and treat a narrow win as "no clear winner" until a bigger run agrees.

**Things change over time.** A model update, a price change, or new kinds of customer questions can flip last month's winner. Re-run the same experiment on a schedule with the rule unchanged, and recheck cost per success against your current price list.

**No code check for the result.** Some tasks have no clear end state to look up, like "write a helpful reply." Then you might grade with an LLM judge, which is a second model that scores the answers. Judges can be wrong or favor longer answers, so check a sample of their grades by hand before you trust the verdict.

learn:term.a:
A **baseline** is the thing you compare against. It's your "normal" before you try something new.

Think of testing a new route to work. Your usual route is the baseline. You time both routes. The new one only counts as better if it beats your usual time. A time on its own, like "22 minutes", tells you nothing until you know what you normally get.

In this lesson, the baseline is **one agent**. It's the simpler, cheaper design. The team has to prove it's worth the extra effort.

In the example, one agent passed every time on 12 of 20 questions, at $0.04 per success. That's the bar. The team passed every time on 15 of 20. That's 3 more in 20, or 1.5 more in 10 (a gain of 0.15). You can only see that gain because you have the baseline to subtract from.

The baseline also shows the price of the team. It costs $0.35 per success against the baseline's $0.04.

In the code, the baseline is the `one-agent` design. It answers the same questions as the team designs.

judge.notes: No real problems. The 'simpler, cheaper' description of one agent is a mild inference, but the example's $0.04 cost supports it. The answer is about 180 words.

check:0:1.q: Why not “Move every helper to a smaller model, then reru…”?
check:0:1.a:
That option gets two things right. Smaller models usually do cost less. And rerunning the eval (your test set that checks the answers are still good) is the right safety check after any change.

What it misses is that you are guessing. Every span is called `"agent"`, so the trace only shows one big total. You can't tell which helper is using most of the 50,000 tokens.

Swapping every helper at once causes three problems:

- **Little gain from some helpers.** Some helpers might use very few tokens, so shrinking them saves almost nothing.
